summary: C reads and writes files through the stdio library using a FILE * stream. You open a file with a mode, read or write with formatted, character, line, or binary functions, move the position indicator if needed, and close the stream.

sections.heading: Opening and closing
sections.body: `fopen(path, mode)` returns a FILE * or NULL on failure; always test it and report errors with `perror`. Close with `fclose` to flush buffers and release the descriptor.

sections.heading: Modes
bullets: Add "b" for binary ("rb", "wb"); it only matters on systems that translate newlines, like Windows.

sections.heading: Reading and writing text
bullets: Loop on the return value, not on `feof`: `while (fgets(line, sizeof line, f)) { ... }`.

sections.heading: Binary I/O
sections.body: `fread(ptr, size, count, f)` and `fwrite(ptr, size, count, f)` move raw bytes and return the number of items transferred. Writing whole structs is quick but not portable across padding, endianness, or compilers.

sections.heading: Positioning
bullets: `rewind(f)`: back to the start and clear error flags.

sections.body: Functions return EOF or a short count on trouble. Distinguish end-of-file from error with `feof(f)` and `ferror(f)`, and inspect `errno` / `perror` for the reason. Check `fclose` and `fflush` results when writing important data, since buffered writes can fail late.
stdio buffers output: line-buffered for terminals, fully buffered for files. `fflush(f)` forces a flush; `setvbuf` changes the mode. A crash before flush loses buffered data.
Three streams are open at start. Errors belong on stderr (unbuffered) so they are visible even when stdout is redirected. `freopen` rebinds a stream to a file.
`open`, `read`, `write`, `close` operate on integer descriptors with no stdio buffering and are used for sockets, pipes, and devices. `fileno(f)` and `fdopen(fd, mode)` convert between the two.

takeaways: Open with fopen, always test for NULL, close with fclose.
Choose text functions (fgets, fprintf) or binary (fread, fwrite) deliberately.
Loop on read return values, not on feof.
Output is buffered; flush or close to persist it.
